notes:
I've written notes on all 18 verses below. A few limits first:

- **Tradition differences:** the sources I found show only one clear split, over the Lord's Supper in v. 8 (and the meal in v. 11). That debate is Catholic against Protestant. I found nothing showing Protestant traditions disagreeing with each other on this chapter.
- **Not found:** nothing from Bible Odyssey, the Orthodox site (oca.org), Lutheran, Pentecostal or Wesleyan sites. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out.
- **Labels:** I only note a commentator's tradition where the page states it.

**Whole chapter**
- The NET Bible notes call this chapter the high point of Exodus in many ways, because God makes the Sinai covenant here. They split it into four parts: the call to worship (1–2), the worshippers made holy (3–8), the covenant confirmed (9–11) and Moses' meeting with God (12–18). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Guzik calls the chapter the "signing" of the Mosaic covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary says some scholars think vv. 1–2 belong after v. 8, but no change is needed: God gave the instructions first and Moses carried them out after the people agreed. Nadab and Abihu were Aaron's two eldest sons and would have been priests after him, had they not later sinned with "strange fire." The group worshipped "at a distance" because they were less holy than Moses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html
- NET: these 74 men went part way up and bowed down, while Moses went on alone. NET compares Moses' role as go-between to Christ's, and says bowing "far off" shows how fearsome God's presence was. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Moses had special access, so God spoke to Moses and Moses spoke to the nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- One commentary on StudyLight says Moses alone drawing near makes him a type of Christ, who, as the high priest, entered alone into the most holy place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-7.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Israel may have been badly overconfident, not grasping how demanding God's law is. On the other hand, a people just terrified at Sinai could hardly do anything but agree. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Pulpit: crowds swept up in strong feeling make promises they later struggle to keep, so Moses asked for more than a spoken yes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html
- NET reads the Hebrew verb as "we are willing to do." On this reading the people were not boasting that they would certainly obey. NET adds that the Ten Commandments may not be included here because the people had already heard them directly. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God's words had to be written down, not left to memory. There was also one covenant for the whole nation, not a private deal for each person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Clarke: Moses builds an altar, probably of turf, as was commanded, Exodus 20:24, and erects twelve pillars, no doubt of unhewn stone. The altar itself represented the throne of God; the twelve stones, the twelve tribes of Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/exodus-24.html
- NET: standing stones like these marked treaties, visions, boundaries or graves. Here they serve, with the altar, as a place of worship. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print

**v. 5**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the young men were not first-born sons (the view of the ancient Aramaic translation, Onkelos), nor Aaron's sons (Augustine's view). They simply acted as servants of Moses, and Moses himself did the priestly work with the blood. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-24.html
- Pulpit gives both possibilities and adds that young men were probably picked because they could handle struggling animals. Guzik, quoting Cole, makes the same practical point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Barnes: The blood which sealed the covenant was the blood of burnt offerings and peace offerings. The sin-offering Leviticus 4:0 had not yet been instituted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-8.html

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry: the blood on the altar signifies the people's dedicating themselves, their lives, and beings, to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm
- Precept Austin sees two sides to the blood: The blood on the altar symbolizes God's forgiveness and acceptance of the offering; the blood on the people points to a blood oath that binds them in obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-24-commentary
- Clarke: sprinkling both the altar and the people showed that both GOD and THEY were mutually bound by this covenant. GOD was bound to the PEOPLE to support, defend, and save them; the PEOPLE were bound to GOD to fear, love, and serve him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/exodus-24.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the Hebrew verb here means to throw or swing the blood, not to sprinkle. They also reject the idea that the rite copied pagan treaty customs where the two parties mixed their own blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-8.htm

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: this is the first "book" actually mentioned as written in the narrative of the Bible, the seed of Holy Scripture. Guzik, quoting Thomas, calls it "doubtless the germ of the Old Testament." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Guzik: God would not bargain over the covenant's terms, and he would not force it on anyone either. The people had to respond freely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- NET: the people now add a second verb ("and obey"), meaning "we want to obey." Their promise is more binding this time because blood confirms it. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print

**v. 8**
- **Who was sprinkled?** Commentators disagree:
  - Pulpit: the people's leaders, standing at the head of each tribe, not two million people. It rejects the idea that only the pillars were sprinkled, citing Hebrews 9:19. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: probably on the twelve pillars, as representing the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-8.htm
  - Coffman: Note that none was sprinkled on the pillars. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-7.html
- **What the blood means:** Guzik says There was nothing "magical" about blood. It stands for life, one life given for another. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Precept Austin: by accepting the blood, Israel was in effect saying it was willing to die if it broke the covenant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-24-commentary
- Pulpit: the two parties shared one blood and so entered a kind of "sacramental union." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html
- **Link to Jesus' words at the Last Supper:** NET says "blood of the covenant" means the blood that ratifies the covenant, and calls the parallel with Matt 26:28 and 1 Cor 11:25 "striking." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Matthew Henry: Jesus seemed to allude to this solemnity when, in the institution of the Lord's supper, he said, This cup is the New Testament (or covenant) in my blood. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm
- **Catholic and Protestant views of the Supper:**
  - Catholic Answers (catholic.com) argues that by saying "blood of the covenant," Jesus meant the Last Supper to be for the New Covenant what this sprinkling at Sinai was for the Old: the ratifying ceremony. It says this supports the real, substantial blood of Christ in the cup. https://www.catholic.com/video/is-the-eucharist-really-the-body-blood-of-jesus
  - The same site reports the opposing Protestant argument from the apologist James White. He points out that the covenant blood at Sinai came from a slain sacrifice, not a living person, and uses this to argue for a non-literal reading. Catholic Answers replies that this does not disprove transubstantiation. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-wine-is-jesus-blood
  - A Gospel Coalition article (Themelios journal) sees Exodus 24:6–8 as the background to Jesus' covenant words and calls the bread and cup an "acted parable." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/how-jesus-understood-the-last-supper-a-parable-in-action/

**v. 9**
- Keil & Delitzsch: made holy by the covenant blood, Israel could now go up and see God, though only through its representatives, since the whole nation could not physically fit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-24.html
- Pulpit warns that even after this vision, Aaron soon made the golden calf and Nadab and Abihu died for disobeying. Their sin was greater because of the privilege they had wasted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-24.html

**v. 10**
- **What did they see?**
  - Guzik: at most God's footstool. Most likely a heavenly vision like Isaiah's or Ezekiel's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
  - Matthew Henry: they saw something of which no image nor picture could be made, and yet enough to satisfy them that God was with them of a truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-10.html
  - Pulpit: the words can scarcely mean less than that they saw with their bodily eyes some appearance of the Divine being. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-10.htm
  - Clarke: only an appearance, with no personal likeness (citing Deuteronomy 4:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-10.html
  - Gill: the mention of feet shows that there was a visible form, and that human. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-10.htm
- **The "sapphire":** Ellicott says it is probably lapis lazuli. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-10.htm
- Trapp (quoted by Guzik): God had turned the bricks of their slavery into sapphire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):** S. R. Driver read it as "they saw the place where God stood," to protect the idea that God cannot be seen. U. Cassuto saw little difference between "they saw God" and "God appeared." The old Greek translation (Septuagint) adds "the place where he stood." What the text describes is what someone lying face-down could see. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print

**v. 11**
- **"Did not lay His hand":**
  - Barnes: He did not strike them. People believed no one could see God and live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-11.htm
  - Clarke lists three readings: God did not cover them with his hand, did not give them the gift of prophecy, or did not kill them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-11.html
  - Calvin rejects the prophecy reading as violently distorted. He takes the meal as a solemn banquet, which was a part or appendage of a sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-11.html
  - Guzik takes the phrase as a sign that something was still missing: this was not a face-to-face meeting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- **Who appeared?** Pulpit: It is generally supposed that, in all such cases, it was the Second Person of the Blessed Trinity who condescended to show himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-11.htm
- NET says some Christian interpreters take it as the pre-incarnate Christ. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- **The meal:** Ellicott calls it a precious forecast of the Christian's highest privilege—the realisation of the presence of God in the sacred feast of the Holy Communion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-11.htm
- NET: this was the covenant meal from the peace offering, showing peace with God. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- F. B. Meyer (quoted by Guzik): some eat and drink without seeing God, some see God without eating and drinking, and some do both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/

**v. 12**
- NET: this is the first mention of the stone tablets. Now that the commands have been agreed and ratified, God will write them on stone. The words "the law and commandments" explain what is on the tablets rather than adding something extra. The final verb means "so that you may teach them." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Matthew Henry reads "be there" as "expect to stay a long time." Those that would have communion with God must not only come to ordinances, but they must abide by them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Joshua began as Moses' assistant, first in battle and now in spiritual things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Matthew Henry, following Bishop Pearson, sees Joshua as a type of Christ, because without Jesus... there is no looking into the secrets of heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Aaron and Hur had proved themselves before (Exodus 17), yet they did not guard the camp well, as later chapters show. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- NET: telling us how Moses prepared for his absence makes the people's and Aaron's guilt in chapter 32 heavier. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: The people stood below, as in the "outer court," the elders in the "holy place," Moses, as a type of Christ, in "the holy of holies." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-16.htm

**v. 15**
- Matthew Henry: the cloud was a sign of God's presence, for he so shows himself to us as at the same time to conceal himself from us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm

**v. 16**
- **"Settled":** NET says the verb means "dwelt." The term "Shekinah glory" comes from it, and so does the word for the tabernacle (mishkan), pointing ahead to the next chapters. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Guzik, quoting Kaiser, links the word to John 1:14, where the Word "tabernacled" among us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- **The seventh day:** Clarke thinks the seventh day was the Sabbath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-16.html
- Poole gives several possible reasons for the wait: to train Moses' humility, to prepare him gradually, or because it was the Sabbath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-16.htm
- Matthew Henry: communion with God is worth waiting for. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm
- Pulpit: Moses was no doubt... occupied during the six days in continual prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/24-16.htm

**v. 17**
- NET: the fire showed God accepting their sacrifice. The vision of glory confirmed the authority of the Law. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
- Guzik: the people could see neither God nor Moses, so God gave them a visible reminder of his presence for those 40 days. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-24/
- Constable: the sight should have given the Israelites greater respect for God's revelation than they demonstrated later. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-16.html

**v. 18**
- Matthew Henry thinks the six days were not part of the forty. He says God could have said everything in one day but kept Moses longer for solemnity. We are hereby taught to spend much time in communion with God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-16.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_024.cfm
- Constable: during the 40 days God gave Moses the tablets and the plans for the tabernacle, because God purposed to dwell among His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/24-16.html
- NET, citing the Jewish commentator B. Jacob: Moses stayed on earth yet stood like a heavenly servant before God, eating and drinking nothing. NET also compares the scene to the Transfiguration and to believers waiting for Christ's return in the clouds. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=24&mode=print
